```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
```

```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

The distribution of the site effects is the `true_dist` argument of a design.
Six distributions are built in. Each is standardized, so that `sigma_tau`
means the same thing for all of them, and a distribution of your own can be
supplied as a function. The last section adds site-level covariates.

## The built-in distributions

`true_dist` names the distribution, and the list `theta_G` holds the
parameters of its shape. Both are arguments of `multisitedgp_design()`, so the
presets, `sim_multisite()`, and `sim_meta()` take them too. The grand mean
`tau` and the cross-site standard deviation `sigma_tau` are separate arguments
and apply to every distribution. Every `theta_G` entry in the table is
required, except `slab_shape`.

| `true_dist` | Shape | `theta_G` entries |
|-----------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `"Gaussian"` | normal (the default) | none |
| `"StudentT"` | Student $t$: symmetric, heavy tails | `nu` (above 2) |
| `"SkewN"` | skew-normal: skewed, light tails | `slant` (any number) |
| `"ALD"` | asymmetric Laplace: skewed, sharp peak | `rho` (between 0.05 and 0.95) |
| `"Mixture"` | mixture of two normal components | `delta` (above 0), `eps` (between 0 and 1), `ups` (above 0) |
| `"PointMassSlab"` | point mass at the grand mean with a continuous slab around it | `pi0` (between 0 and 1), `slab_shape` (`"Gaussian"` by default, or `"Laplace"`) |

`gen_effects()` draws the site effects alone, which is the first step of
`sim_multisite()` and `sim_meta()`. The code below draws 100,000 site effects
from each distribution at the defaults, `tau = 0` and `sigma_tau = 0.2`.

```{r draws}
shapes <- list(
  Gaussian = list(),
  StudentT = list(nu = 5),
  SkewN = list(slant = 5),
  ALD = list(rho = 0.3),
  Mixture = list(delta = 5, eps = 0.3, ups = 2),
  PointMassSlab = list(pi0 = 0.3)
)
set.seed(1)
draws <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(shapes), function(d) {
  x <- gen_effects(J = 1e5, true_dist = d, theta_G = shapes[[d]])
  data.frame(true_dist = factor(d, names(shapes)), x[c("z_j", "tau_j")])
}))
head(draws, 3)
```

`z_j` is the standardized site effect, a draw from the distribution scaled to
mean 0 and variance 1. `tau_j` is the site effect, `tau + sigma_tau * z_j`. In
the first row, $0.2 \times (-0.626) = -0.125$.

```{r densities, fig.cap = "Each histogram has mean 0 and standard deviation 0.2, like the normal curve drawn over it. Only the shape differs."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(draws, aes(tau_j)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 0.04, fill = "grey") +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(sd = 0.2)) +
  facet_wrap(~true_dist, scales = "free_y") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.8, 0.8)) +
  labs(x = "Site effect", y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The Student $t$ histogram is higher than the normal curve at the center and
lower on the shoulders. Its heavier tails are too thin to see at this scale.
The skew-normal and asymmetric Laplace histograms peak left of 0 and have a
long right tail. The mixture has a second, lower mode near 0.26. In the last
panel the bar at 0 contains the 30 percent of sites in the point mass.

## Each distribution

### Gaussian

The normal distribution is the default and has no `theta_G` entries. Most
multilevel and random-effects models assume it, so it serves as the reference
when other shapes are studied.

### Student t

A $t$ distribution with `nu` degrees of freedom is symmetric with heavier
tails than the normal, so a few sites lie far from the grand mean. Its
variance is finite only for `nu` above 2. At 4 or less a simulation gives a
warning, because the standard deviation of the simulated site effects is then
below `sigma_tau` in most data sets and far above it in a few. The line gives
the share of the 100,000 draws that lie more than three standard deviations
from the grand mean.

```{r tails}
round(tapply(abs(draws$z_j) > 3, draws$true_dist, mean), 4)
```

With `nu = 5` the share is 1.2 percent, against 0.3 percent for the normal.
Use this distribution to see how an estimator copes with outlying sites.

### Skew-normal

`slant` is the parameter $\alpha$ of the skew-normal density
$2 \phi(x) \Phi(\alpha x)$ of Azzalini [-@azzalini1985class]. A positive value
gives a longer right tail, a negative value a longer left tail, and 0 gives
the normal distribution. Its skewness stays between $-1$ and 1, so use this
distribution for moderate asymmetry without outlying sites.

### Asymmetric Laplace

The asymmetric Laplace distribution [@yu2005three] has a sharp peak and an
exponential tail on each side. `rho` is the probability that a site effect
lies below the peak, so the right tail is the longer one for `rho` below 0.5.
Use it when most sites are near one typical effect and the exceptions lie far
out on one side. In the output shown under Student t, 1.5 percent of its sites
are beyond three standard deviations, against 0.8 percent for the skew-normal.

### Two-component mixture

The mixture has two normal components, and a site belongs to the second with
probability `eps`. `delta` is the distance between the component means and
`ups` is the standard deviation of the second component, both in units of the
standard deviation of the first. `gen_effects()` returns the component of each
site in the column `latent_component`, which `sim_multisite()` does not keep.

```{r mixture}
set.seed(1)
mix <- gen_effects(
  J = 1000, true_dist = "Mixture", theta_G = list(delta = 5, eps = 0.3, ups = 2)
)
print(mix, n = 4)
table(mix$latent_component)
round(tapply(mix$tau_j, mix$latent_component, mean), 3)
round(tapply(mix$tau_j, mix$latent_component, sd), 3)
```

Site 4 is in the second component, which has 304 of the 1,000 sites. Its mean
is 0.374 above that of the first, about five times the first component's
standard deviation of 0.078, and its own standard deviation is twice as large.
Use the mixture for two kinds of sites, or with a small `eps` for a few sites
that stand apart. `preset_jebs_paper()` has these values, and
`preset_twin_towers()` has two equal components.

### Point mass with a slab

With probability `pi0` the standardized site effect is exactly 0, so the site
effect equals the grand mean. The other sites are spread around the same point
by a normal distribution, or by a Laplace distribution with
`slab_shape = "Laplace"`. With `tau = 0` this is a treatment that does nothing
in a share `pi0` of the sites.

```{r pmslab}
dat <- sim_multisite(
  true_dist = "PointMassSlab", theta_G = list(pi0 = 0.3), seed = 1
)
dat
sum(dat$tau_j == 0)
```

Sites 1 and 5 are in the point mass. Their `z_j` and `tau_j` are exactly 0,
and their estimates `tau_j_hat` are not, because an estimate still has
sampling error. In all, 12 of the 50 sites have an effect of exactly 0, where
15 are expected. `theta_G` also accepts `mu_slab` and `sigma_slab`, but the
standardization cancels them and they do not change the data. A slab that is
not centered on the point mass needs a user-supplied function.

## Standardization

Every distribution is shifted and scaled to mean 0 and variance 1 before
`sigma_tau` is applied. A $t$ variable with 5 degrees of freedom, for example,
has variance $5/3$. Used as it is, a design with `sigma_tau = 0.2` would
produce site effects with a standard deviation of 0.26. `gen_effects()`
therefore multiplies the draws by $\sqrt{3/5}$. `sigma_tau` is then the
cross-site standard deviation under every `true_dist`, and a change of
distribution changes the shape and nothing else.

```{r standardization}
moments <- function(z) c(mean = mean(z), variance = var(z))
round(t(sapply(split(draws$z_j, draws$true_dist), moments)), 3)
round(tapply(draws$tau_j, draws$true_dist, sd), 3)
```

In 100,000 draws the means of `z_j` are within 0.005 of 0 and the variances
within 0.01 of 1. The standard deviations of `tau_j` are all 0.2 to two
decimals. This holds for the distribution, not for each data set. In the 50
sites of the point-mass example the header reads target 0.200, realized 0.178,
and the heavier the tails, the more the realized value varies.

## A user-supplied distribution

`true_dist = "User"` takes the distribution from a function, `g_fn`. The
function has an argument `J`, the number of sites, and returns `J` numbers.
Entries of `theta_G` are passed to it as further arguments. `g_returns` says
what the numbers are. With `"standardized"` (the default) they are draws of
`z_j`, and the function must give them mean 0 and variance 1. With `"raw"`
they are the site effects `tau_j` themselves.

The example is an exponential distribution. Every site effect is positive,
most are small, and a few are large. An exponential variable with rate 1 has
mean 1 and variance 1, so subtracting 1 standardizes it.

```{r user-standardized}
g_std <- function(J) rexp(J) - 1
dat <- sim_multisite(
  true_dist = "User", g_fn = g_std, tau = 0.2, sigma_tau = 0.2, seed = 1
)
dat
min(dat$tau_j)
```

The site effects are $0.2 + 0.2 z_j$ and `z_j` is never below $-1$, so no site
effect is negative. The smallest of the 50 is 0.007. The same distribution
with `g_returns = "raw"` is an exponential distribution with mean 0.2 for the
site effects themselves.

```{r user-raw}
g_raw <- function(J) rexp(J, rate = 5)
dat_raw <- sim_multisite(
  true_dist = "User", g_fn = g_raw, g_returns = "raw",
  tau = 0.2, sigma_tau = 0.2, seed = 1
)
all.equal(dat_raw$tau_j, dat$tau_j)
```

The two designs give the same site effects. With `"raw"`, `tau` and
`sigma_tau` do not enter the site effects. They still define `z_j`, as
`(tau_j - tau) / sigma_tau`, and enter the diagnostics, so set them to the
mean and the standard deviation of the distribution that `g_fn` returns.

With `"standardized"`, the function is called a second time with `J = 100000`.
This check warns if the mean of those draws is more than 0.1 from 0 or their
variance more than 0.1 from 1. It does not change the data. `gen_effects()`
skips it with `audit_g = FALSE`, and `sim_multisite()` and `sim_meta()` always
run it.

```{r audit}
set.seed(1)
x <- g_raw(1e5)
c(mean = mean(x), variance = var(x))
```

These are the two numbers the check computes. `g_raw` without
`g_returns = "raw"` fails on both and gives the warning.

## Site-level covariates

A design can make the site effects depend on site-level covariates. `data` is
a data frame with one row per site, `formula` is a one-sided formula in its
columns, and `beta` holds the coefficients. The site effect is then
$\tau_j = \tau + x_j'\beta + \sigma_\tau z_j$, where $x_j$ holds the covariate
values of site $j$. The coefficient of the intercept may be left out of `beta`
and is then 0.

```{r covariate}
sites <- data.frame(urban = rep(c(0, 1), each = 25))
dat <- sim_multisite(
  J = 50, formula = ~urban, beta = 0.2, data = sites, seed = 1
)
dat
all.equal(dat$tau_j, 0.2 * dat$urban + 0.2 * dat$z_j)
c(residual = sd(dat$tau_j - 0.2 * dat$urban), marginal = sd(dat$tau_j))
```

The data have an eighth column, `urban`, copied from `sites`. The
`all.equal()` line confirms the formula, with `tau = 0`, `beta = 0.2`, and
`sigma_tau = 0.2`. `sigma_tau` is now the standard deviation of the site
effects around the covariate part, that is, among sites with the same
covariate values. Its realized value, labeled residual in the output, is
0.166, the number in the header. The marginal standard deviation, that of all
50 site effects, is 0.187. In the population its square is $\sigma_\tau^2$
plus the variance of $x_j'\beta$, so it is the larger of the two.

In `summary()`, rows labeled residual are computed from `z_j` and rows labeled
marginal from `tau_j`. With `g_returns = "raw"` the covariate part is not
added, because `g_fn` then returns the complete site effects.
